# Brief: review the Flange Street lease before we commit to another five years

The Flange Street unit is our second-largest fixed cost and the lease runs out
in fourteen months. The landlord has already been in touch about renewal, which
is earlier than they need to be, and that usually means they expect us to stay.

## What the unit does for us

It holds the overflow stock that will not fit at the main site, and it houses
the small team who handle returns. Neither function is glamorous and both are
load-bearing: returns processing has a two-day service commitment attached to it
and the overflow is what keeps the main site's aisles clear during peak.

The building itself is unremarkable and adequate. The roof was repaired two
years ago at the landlord's cost, the loading door works, and the office end is
tired but functional.

## The question

Renew, renegotiate, or move. All three are live and I have no preferred answer.

Renewal is the cheap option in effort and the expensive one if the rent review
lands where the landlord's early approach suggests it will.

Renegotiation is the interesting one. We have been a reliable tenant for nine
years in a street where two units have stood empty for eighteen months, and that
is a stronger position than we have historically played.

Moving is a real option and it is the one that has never been costed. There is
space at the northern estate at a headline rent well below what we pay, and the
usual reason we dismiss it — the distance from the main site — is worth
examining rather than repeating.

## What to produce

- The true cost of staying, including the rent review's likely landing point,
  the dilapidations position at the end of the current term, and the service
  charge trajectory over the last five years.
- The true cost of moving, including the fit-out, the fortnight of disruption to
  returns processing, and the effect on the eleven people who work there — six of
  whom walk to work and would not be able to.
- The negotiating position, written as a position: what we want, what we will
  trade, and what we walk away over.
- A recommendation, and the reasoning, in a form the board can read in ten
  minutes.

## Constraints

- Nothing said to the landlord until the costing is done. Their early approach
  is an invitation to negotiate before we know our own numbers, and that is the
  worst moment to start.
- The returns service commitment does not move. Whatever we do has to keep it,
  which rules out any option with a gap between vacating and occupying.
- The eleven people are the part I care most about getting right. Whatever the
  numbers say, I want the human cost stated plainly and separately rather than
  folded into a total.

## Timing

Eight weeks. That leaves a year of runway, which is what turns a negotiation
into a real one — the landlord knows as well as we do that a tenant with three
months left has no position at all.

## Who else to talk to

The returns team lead has run that operation for six years and has a list of
things wrong with the building that has never been asked for. Ask for it — half
of it will be trivial and the other half is the fit-out specification for
wherever we end up.

Our agent will have a view and an interest, and the two are not the same. Take
the view, discount the interest, and get a second opinion on the rent review's
likely landing point from somebody who is not being paid on the transaction.
